The notes below come only from the long excerpts the search engine returned for Enduring Word (Guzik), StudyLight, Bible Hub, Blue Letter Bible and Precept Austin. Those excerpts cover part 1 (the traditional reading) well, but leave gaps on some verses.

**What's missing:**
- I couldn't reach any Catholic or Orthodox sources (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org).
- I couldn't reach any modern scholarship (netbible, bibleodyssey).
- I couldn't reach the denominational sites (ligonier, gty, seedbed, lcms, 1517, ag.org and the rest).
- I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.

So the "differences" notes only show where named commentators disagree. Where a tradition is given, it's the site's own label (for example, StudyLight tags Gill as "Calvinist, Baptist" and Ellicott as "Arminian, Anglican").

---

**v. 1**
- Festus going to Jerusalem after only three days suggests he was a good, energetic leader. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/
- Gill says Festus probably came by sea and landed at Caesarea. Joppa was nearer to Jerusalem, but Caesarea, the harbour Herod built, was safer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-25.html
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that "province" uses the same word as Acts 23:34. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/25.htm

**v. 2**
- Gill: some ancient copies read "chief priests," meaning the whole body of priests. "Chief of the Jews" means the rulers and elders of the Sanhedrin. They moved quickly, hoping a new governor would want to please them before he learned how they operated. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-25.html
- Guzik: two years on, Paul's case still mattered to them. His comfortable imprisonment in Caesarea was God's protective custody, and also a season of rest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/

**v. 3**
- Guzik: they knew a fair trial would clear Paul, so they wanted an ambush instead. He quotes Boice: in Acts 23 the zealots started the plot, but now the leaders themselves were behind it, a sign of growing corruption. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/
- Gill: they hid their real aim, perhaps planning to use the same forty men as before (Acts 23:12). The episode shows their malice and God's care for Paul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-25.html
- Poole: what they asked for looked like justice, but they framed it as a personal favour to make it easier to get. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/acts/25.htm
- Precept Austin: the roughly 60-mile road from Caesarea had rough ground well suited to an ambush. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-25-commentary
- R. Tuck (Pulpit Homiletics): they took advantage of a new governor's wish to please his subjects. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/acts/25.htm
- The Pulpit Commentaries call the plot "religious bigotry" with little chance of success, since Roman soldiers didn't usually lose their prisoners. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-25.html

**vv. 4–5**
- Guzik: we can't tell whether Festus knew about the plot. Either way, his refusal was another way God protected Paul. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/
- Gill calls the answer wise and prudent: Paul was already properly guarded in Caesarea, and Festus was going back soon. Gill reads "able" as those who had the time, means and ability to prove a charge. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-25.html
- Pulpit: Festus wasn't just stating where Paul was; he was declaring his decision to keep him there for trial. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/25.htm
- Cambridge Greek Testament: the oldest texts read "anything amiss" (literally "out of the way"), which the Revised Version follows. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/acts-25.html

**v. 6**
- Gill lists the manuscript and translation evidence for "no more than eight or ten days." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-25.html

**v. 7**
- Gill: Paul's conduct before and after his conversion was blameless, so his enemies couldn't prove a single charge. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-25.html
- Pulpit Homiletics (quoting an older writer): this time the Jews had no hired speaker, so the hearing turned into angry shouting. They seem to have brought no witnesses, and Paul knew a Roman judge wouldn't act on unsupported accusations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/acts/25.htm
- Precept Austin: the word for "prove" means to demonstrate by argument. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-25-commentary

**v. 8**
- Barclay: Paul's answer shows the three charges were heresy, sacrilege and sedition. From the Jews' point of view the first was true, though irrelevant to Roman law; the other two were deliberate lies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/acts-25.html
- Gill takes each point in turn:
  - Paul kept the moral law, and for peace's sake also kept the ceremonial law, which he knew had been abolished.
  - He didn't profane the temple.
  - He wasn't guilty of sedition against Caesar.
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-25.html
- Cambridge Greek Testament: the accusers would lean hardest on the sedition charge. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/acts-25.html
- Matthew Henry: preaching Christ, "the end of the law," was no offence against the law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/acts/25.htm
- Preacher's Homiletical: what Paul preached was a legitimate outgrowth of the Hebrew faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-25.html

**v. 9**
- Guzik: Paul's citizenship apparently meant Festus could only ask, not order, a move. If Festus knew of the plot, he was knowingly sending Paul into an ambush. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/
- Precept Austin quotes Wiersbe: a Roman judge couldn't move a case without the defendant's consent. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-25-commentary
- Gill: Festus meant a trial before the Sanhedrin with himself present, after the Jews kept pressing him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-25.html
- Church Pulpit Commentary (Anglican): since there was no case, Paul should have been acquitted. The wish to please the Jews stopped Festus, just as it had stopped Felix. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/acts-25.html
- Lowell Johnson: Festus reversed his earlier position and went against his conscience for personal gain. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-acts-lowell-johnson

**v. 10**
- Gill and the Pulpit Commentary: it is "Caesar's judgment seat" because Festus judged in Caesar's name. As a citizen, Paul had a right to be tried there and not by the Sanhedrin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-25.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/25.htm
- Poole: Paul had good reason to distrust the judges, the place and the journey. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/acts/25.htm
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown: Paul's reply implies he understood Festus to be proposing to hand him over to the Sanhedrin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_025.cfm
- Church Pulpit: we owe it to our good name to defend our integrity against false witnesses. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/acts-25.html

**v. 11**
- **Meaning of the words.** Ellicott and the Cambridge Greek Testament: "deliver me" literally means "give me up as a favour." This shows Paul saw through Festus's show of fairness. https://biblehub.com/acts/25-11.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/acts-25.html
- **Paul's reasons for appealing.**
  - Gill gives three: the governor's leaning toward the Jews, Paul's likely knowledge of the ambush, and "chiefly" the vision of Acts 23:11. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-25.html
  - Precept Austin and Bible Hub also tie it to that promise. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-25-commentary ; https://biblehub.com/q/Why_does_Paul_appeal_to_Caesar.htm
  - Guzik: Paul saw through the plot, either by supernatural knowledge or God-given common sense. He was confident a fair trial would clear him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/
- **Roman law.** Clarke: citizens could appeal even before sentence. The Julian law punished officials who harmed a citizen who had appealed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/25-11.html
  - Barclay: the appeal didn't apply to murderers, pirates or bandits caught in the act. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/acts-25.html
- **Can a Christian claim legal rights?**
  - Calvin: once Paul has said he won't refuse death if guilty, he freely uses human help. We too may seek help from the laws without being "superstitious." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/25-11.html
  - Barnes: Jesus asserted his rights at his trial (John 18:23). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/25-11.html
  - Preacher's Homiletical raises Matthew 5:39 (non-resistance). Its answer: Paul seeks self-preservation, not revenge, and that isn't forbidden. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-25.html
  - Guzik: Paul sometimes gave up his rights (Philippi, 1 Cor 9) and sometimes stood on them, as here. https://enduringword.com/standing-on-our-rights/
- **Disagreement over Nero.**
  - Guzik: Nero was considered just in his first five years, so Paul had no reason yet to expect hostility. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/
  - Church Pulpit (Anglican): Nero was as cruel as any ruler. It asks why Paul appealed to him "knowing his character only too well," and calls the appeal "the last refuge of oppressed innocency." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/acts-25.html
- **Was the appeal right?** Constable: nothing in the New Testament suggests it went against God's will. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/25-11.html
- **Early church.** Preacher's Homiletical cites Athenagoras, an early Christian apologist, as a parallel: Christians ask no favour, only punishment if convicted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-25.html

**v. 12**
- Gill: the "council" were Festus's Roman advisers, not the Sanhedrin. His reply may carry some resentment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-25.html
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown hear an implied "see if you fare better." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_025.cfm
- Plumptre (in Preacher's Homiletical) hears "something like a sneer," as Festus knew the long delays ahead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-25.html
- Others think Festus was relieved:
  - The Pulpit Commentary cites Pliny sending citizen Christians to Rome as a parallel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/25.htm
  - Coffman: it got Festus "off the hook." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/25-11.html
  - Precept Austin agrees he was likely relieved. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-25-commentary

**v. 13**
- Gill: this is Agrippa II, son of the Herod Agrippa who killed James (Acts 12). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-25.html
- Barclay: his small kingdom, which included Galilee and Peraea, depended on Rome's goodwill, so he made courtesy visits to new governors. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/acts-25.html
- Plumptre: Bernice was his sister and Drusilla's sister. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-25.html
- Cambridge Greek Testament discusses the reading "having saluted." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/acts-25.html

**v. 14**
- Guzik: Festus, new to the job, seemed confused, though the lack of evidence alone was reason to acquit. This was a hearing, not a trial, since Agrippa had no jurisdiction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/

**vv. 15–16**
- Guzik: the leaders wanted Paul condemned without being heard. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/
- Poole: this is how they had gotten Jesus condemned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/acts/25.htm
- Matthew Henry: this pagan followed the rules of justice, while many Christians judge their brothers hastily. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/acts/25.htm
- The Pulpit Commentaries apply the same rule to private gossip and judgments. They also note that Festus made "a parade of justice" while wanting to be popular. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-25.html
- Plumptre: Festus used the same verb ("give up as a favour") that Paul had used, which shows Paul's remark had hit home. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-25.html

**vv. 17–18**
- Gilbrant (in Precept Austin): "delay" is a legal term for postponing a trial. Festus had expected real crimes, such as extortion, treason or murder. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-25-commentary

**v. 19**
- **"A certain Jesus."**
  - Guzik: the phrase shows how little the powerful knew of Jesus. He quotes Spurgeon on why we must keep preaching him. It also shows Paul preached Christ's death and resurrection, and so the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/
  - Gilbrant: the resurrection was the central issue. Festus neither understood it nor mocked it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-25-commentary
  - The Pulpit Commentaries call the resurrection the central fact of Christianity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-25.html
  - Matthew Henry: one day the whole Roman empire will look trivial next to this question. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/acts/25.htm
- **"Religion" or "superstition"?**
  - The Pulpit Commentary notes Bishop Wordsworth's reading "his own superstition," meaning Paul's. On that view, belief in the resurrection was the "superstition." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/25.htm
  - Matthew Henry: some think Festus meant the Christian religion, much as the Athenians thought of a new god. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_025.cfm
  - Pulpit Homiletics prefers the plain word "religion." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/acts/25.htm
  - Biblical Illustrator: a worldly education sees the Christian faith as superstition. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/25-24.html

**v. 20**
- Poole: Festus's confusion was only a pretext; the real reason was in v. 9. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/acts/25.htm

**v. 21**
- Robertson and Gilbrant: "decision" (diagnosis) is the regular legal word for a thorough examination. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-25-commentary
- Gill: "Augustus" here means Nero. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/25-25.html

**v. 22**
- Pulpit: the Greek imperfect makes this a polite, indirect wish. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/25.htm
- Guzik: this was Paul's third chance to speak before a ruler in Acts 24–26. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/

**v. 23**
- Guzik: this was an event, and Paul had more real dignity than anyone there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-25/
- Barclay pictures the royal purple robes and Festus in his scarlet. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/acts-25.html
- Cambridge Greek Testament: "auditorium" occurs only here in the New Testament (in classical Greek, a lecture room), and "commanders" means officers over a cohort. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/acts-25.html
- Poole: Paul, the chained prisoner, would still rather share Christ's sufferings than their splendour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/acts/25.htm

**v. 24**
- Gill: they wanted his death and nothing else would satisfy them (compare Acts 22:22). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/25-24.html
- Ellicott: "and also here" suggests the Jews of Caesarea joined in. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/25-24.html

**v. 25**
- Preacher's Homiletical: this is valuable evidence that the governor thought Paul innocent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-25.html
- Constable: Luke stresses that Paul's innocence was recognised by Roman authorities, by a Jewish king, and in public. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/26-3.html
- Poole: the Jews' slander only adds to Paul's reputation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/acts/25.htm

**v. 26**
- Gilbrant: "inquiry" (anakrisis) was a legal term for a preliminary hearing. Festus grasped that Paul was innocent but not what his message was. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-25-commentary

**v. 27**
- The Pulpit Commentaries: Festus is sensible here, but a show of fairness means nothing unless rulers learn the facts. They contrast Pilate. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-25.html

**Throughout the chapter (providence)**
- Several writers stress that God was steering events. The Pulpit Commentaries and the Church Pulpit say a Jerusalem trial would have killed Paul, and some of his letters might never have been written. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-25.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/acts-25.html
